column1: “Why should I vote for him again?”
column2: Fair question. The first years were hard, and nobody should pretend otherwise. But the hardest part of the reform is behind us: inflation has fallen from about 34% to under 15%, the naira has steadied, and states now receive far more money. Changing course now risks undoing those gains just as they start to pay off.
column3: Inflation 33.88% (Oct 2024) → 14.63% (Sept 2026), NBS. Naira trading near ₦1,400/$ through 2026; reserves near $50bn; GDP growth 3.89% in Q1 2026.

column2: Many families feel that, and prices really are higher. But the old system was borrowing from tomorrow: petrol subsidy alone was heading for about ₦6.7 trillion in 2023, roughly 70% of federal revenue. That couldn't last. The fix hurt, but the economy is now on firmer ground.
column3: Finance Ministry projection of the full-year 2023 subsidy cost. Avoid saying life is now cheaper; say the economy is more stable.

column1: “He has had his chance. Let someone else try.”
column2: I understand. But the next four years decide whether the sacrifices of the last three pay off. Inflation is falling, reserves are rising and growth has picked up. A new team would likely restart from scratch, and Nigerians would pay for the reforms without collecting the benefits.
column3: GDP grew 3.89% in Q1 2026, up from 3.13% a year earlier (NBS). External reserves rose from about $33bn (2023) to over $50bn (Feb 2026), per CBN.

column1: “I'm not voting at all. My vote doesn't count.”
column2: I hear that a lot. But in 2024 the Supreme Court upheld five opposition governors, so the votes cast at polling units stood. Your vote is still the strongest say you have. Can I help you check that you're on the register?
column3: Kano, Plateau, Abia, Bauchi and Zamfara governors upheld in January 2024. INEC's final voter register is due 15 December 2026.

column1: What are the five headline gains to mention when a voter asks "what has he achieved?"
column2: 1) Inflation more than halved (33.88% → 14.63%). 2) A stable naira. 3) Reserves near $50bn. 4) 1.6m+ student loans. 5) Much higher allocations to states and local governments.
column3: Pick one or two that fit the voter's life. Never list all five on one call.
